doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

title: Gil Fuller, arranger for Dizzy Gillespie
summary: Fuller told Pelote his life story, was proud of his credit, exaggerated, and disparaged Tadd Dameron; they discuss his Moody and Gillespie arrangements.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: You do. And the other interesting person I meet there was also Walter “Gil” Fuller.

The arranger for Dizzy Gillespie. He took a liking to me. I don’t know why. But he sort of took me under his wing, and he took me out to lunch many, many times. And basically he just poured out his life story to me. He felt like he’d been basically forgotten. He was

very proud of the one article that talked about him, Leonard Feather wrote the article in fact, about Gil Fuller. And he was very proud of that article, that at least somebody recognized his talents. And he was telling me all the things he did that he didn’t get credit for, and of course I found out later that he also was a fantastic liar in a lot of ways, and exaggerator, and he exaggerated a lot of his accomplishments. And I won’t say – I mean I don’t know to what degree he did, but I have since found out that certain things he said he did he really didn’t do, or he farmed out certain things to other arrangers, which they all did. Quincy Jones did it, they all kind of did it. He was very opinionated, there were certain people he just did not care for stylistically or whatever. He had a bug up his butt about Tadd Dameron for some reason. He really didn’t think Tadd Dameron was all that great an arranger. And in fact he said to me, “If you listen to ‘Hothouse,’” he says, “really listen to ‘Hothouse,’” he says, “does that sound like Tadd Dameron would have done?” He said, “That sounds more to me like Charlie Parker might have wrote that and Dameron took credit for that” you know. Because he said, you know, “Dameron did things like ‘Good Bait’” [scats] and then he would hum that to me, and then he would say, “now listen to ‘Hot House’ and tell me” [inaudible]. He loved Sy Oliver, he loved, again, a guy named Phil Moore, he was in love with him, he loved Quincy Jones, so Quincy Jones was okay. And he said he did some work for Benny Goodman — oh no, he said he was approached by Benny Goodman to do arrangements for the big band but he turned it down and gave it to Chico O’Farrill. Now I’ve heard Chico O’Farrill talk about that, and not once did he ever mention Gil Fuller giving him that job. So I kind of wonder what that was all about too. So yeah, but Gil was interesting. A lot of what he said was true. I mean a lot of things he said, I mean the whole thing with writing “Things to Come” and stuff like that. I mean, that was all his.
I have a picture of an LP I had, “Last Train from Overbrook.” I think it was James Moody.

Yeah. Well he did the Moody arrangements for the Monterey Jazz Festival. Remember that? There were two albums that came out, because he was in charge of the Monterey Jazz Festival Orchestra for a while, and he did the Gillespie one, and then he did the Moody one. And those were his arrangements. I’ve yet to hear anybody dispute that, so I don’t know. Maybe somebody will at some point. But he said he did those. And they’re wonderful albums, both of them.
